The EDF wrapper div 'body' is treated as the whole work and keyed by the commentaryid. Extended 2026-10-09 with Liber 3, Distinctiones 23-32 (FrMS88-d1e8112), Liber 3 (FrMS88-d1x707), and regeneration of the whole-work entry (FrMS88).

FrMS88-d1e68.summary: Meyronnes' prologue to Book 1 is a sustained treatise in twenty-one questions on the foundations of theological knowledge, organized in three movements. (1) The first principle and the univocity of being (qq. 1–13). Question 1 identifies the first complex principle — 'of anything the affirmation or negation is true, and of nothing both together' — whose subject is being, and argues that it holds formally, univocally, and identically in God and creatures; preserving non-contradiction in God requires a distinction ex natura rei (the formal distinction) between essence and relation, compatible with divine simplicity, and leads into disputes about indivisions, signa originis, and whether the essence could be enjoyed without the persons. Questions 2–5 establish that being has one concept and one formal notion common to God and creatures, by Scotus' argument from the certain and doubtful concept, by sermocinal arguments (degrees of comparison, reduplication, distribution, contradiction, syllogism) and real ones (distinction by posterior modes, opposition, plurality, pure perfection), and show that this univocity is not repugnant to divine perfection. Questions 6–13 specify the mode of univocity: being is not said quidditatively of the simply simple, the primarily diverse, its attributes, or ultimate differences; it is said of the divine essence as a genus is of a difference, not as an essential part; its notion is prescinded from deity; no common quidditative concept can be abstracted from the simply simple; it is univocal to cognized and real being, absolute and respective, substance and accident, and act and objective potency (but not to beings of reason); it is not a genus, nor is God in a genus; it is not predicated by prior and posterior; and only second intentions, transcendental respects, aptitudes, and privations are more common than it. (2) The status of theology (q. 14): theology in itself is a science, but for the wayfarer strictly theological truths are believed, while the metaphysical truths about God can be known scientifically; theology as defense of the faith is the noblest part of metaphysics. (3) The theory of cognition bearing on knowledge of God (qq. 15–21): abstractive cognition terminates at the quiddity in itself through a representative, and the divine essence can be known abstractively without its existence, by an elevated or separated intellect though not naturally by us in this life; intuitive cognition is caused by and terminates at an existing object, so that God can supply its cause but not its terminus and there is no intuition of non-existents, while the particular senses are never deceived (illusions belong to the common sense and imagination); in this life we intuit only our own acts, inferring the soul, its powers, and its habits; whether intuitive vision of God can be granted to a wayfarer depends on whether beatitude lies in intellect or will; and theology is supernaturally revealed, since the intellect, though its adequate object is being, attains God only as being and not under the notion of deity.
claims: There is a unique first complex principle, whose subject is being, and it holds univocally and identically in God and creatures.
Preserving non-contradiction in God requires a formal distinction (ex natura rei) between essence and relation, compatible with divine simplicity.
Being has one concept and one formal notion univocal to God and creatures, and this is not repugnant to divine perfection.
Being is not said quidditatively of the simply simple, the primarily diverse, its attributes, or ultimate differences, and is said of the divine essence as a genus is of a difference.
Being is not a genus, God is not in a genus, and being is not predicated analogically by prior and posterior.
Being is univocal to real and cognized being, absolute and respective, substance and accident, and act and objective potency, but not to beings of reason.
Theology is a science in itself, but for the wayfarer its strictly theological truths are believed; its metaphysical truths about God can be known scientifically.
The divine essence can be known abstractively without its existence, but not under its proper notion by our natural powers in this life.
Intuitive cognition requires an existing object as terminus; God can supply the object's causality but not its terminating role.
The particular senses are not deceived; sensory illusions belong to the common sense and imagination.
In this life only the soul's acts are known intuitively; the soul, its powers, and its habits are known discursively.
Theology is supernaturally revealed because the intellect naturally attains God only as being, not under the notion of deity.

FrMS88-d1e4237.summary: Distinction 37 treats God's presence to creatures in two paired questions, the first on place and the second on time. Question 1 asks whether God is everywhere. Against Isaiah's 'heaven is my seat', it determines that divine ubiquity is neither a being of reason, nor a privation, nor something absolute, nor formally in God; it is a relation of presentiality (respectus praesentialitatis) grounded formally in the creature and directed toward God, illustrated by the soul being whole in the whole body and whole in each part. It then examines four traditional ways of proving that God is everywhere — from immensity, causality, immutability, and coexistence — and finds none of them demonstrative as commonly presented. A new presence can arise through a new relation in the creature without change in God, as when God becomes creator or lord, and a full resolution is deferred to the doctrine of the immobility of place in Book 2. Question 2, built explicitly on the same model, asks whether God is in all time and answers with parallel conclusions: being in time is not a relation of reason, since God is really in time, nor a privation, nor something absolute, nor the same respect as presence in place. God's relation to time is articulated through the presentiality of temporal things to him. Taken together, the distinction treats God's ubiquity and his presence in time as relational predicates founded in creatures, which leaves divine immutability intact.
claims: God is everywhere and in all time, but these are relative predicates grounded in the creature rather than absolute determinations of God.
Divine ubiquity is a respectus praesentialitatis, not a being of reason, a privation, or anything absolute or formally in God.
None of the traditional proofs of divine ubiquity (from immensity, causality, immutability, coexistence) is fully demonstrative as commonly presented.
New presence of God to place or time arises from a new relation in the creature, without change in God.
God's presence in time is distinct from, though parallel to, his presence in place.

FrMS88-d1x63X.summary: PARTIAL: this summary of Book 1 rests on only 2 of its 42 direct divisions, the Prologus and Distinction 37. Distinctions 1–36 and 38–48, which cover among other things the Trinity, the divine attributes, divine knowledge, and divine will, are not yet interpreted and are not represented here. The Prologus lays the epistemological and metaphysical foundations of the commentary. It identifies the first complex principle (non-contradiction joined with excluded middle) and argues that it holds univocally in God and creatures. From this it argues for a formal distinction between divine essence and relation. It establishes the univocity of the concept and formal notion of being and specifies how that univocity works. It defines theology's status as a science in itself but not, in its strictly theological truths, for the wayfarer. It develops a theory of abstractive and intuitive cognition to settle what kind of knowledge of God is naturally or supernaturally possible, and concludes that theology is revealed. Distinction 37 treats God's presence to creatures in place and in time. It holds that ubiquity and presence in time are relations of presentiality grounded in creatures and not absolute determinations of God, and it judges the traditional proofs of ubiquity non-demonstrative as commonly presented. The two covered divisions share a characteristic method: Meyronnes resolves theological predicates by distinguishing formal notions, modes, and relations so as to protect divine simplicity and immutability, and he does not take inherited arguments on trust.
claims: The first complex principle and the univocal concept of being apply to God and creatures alike and ground theological discourse.
A formal distinction between divine essence and relation is required to preserve non-contradiction in God.
Theology is a science in itself, but for the wayfarer its strictly theological truths are revealed and believed.
Predicates such as ubiquity and presence in time are relations grounded in creatures, not absolute determinations of God.

FrMS88.summary: PARTIAL: this summary of Francis of Meyronnes' Commentarius in libros Sententiarum (the 'conflatus', Venice 1519) rests on only 2 of its 4 books, Books 1 and 3, and both of those interpretations are themselves partial. For Book 1 only the Prologus and Distinction 37 are covered; for Book 3, only Distinctions 23–32. Book 2, Book 4, and most of Books 1 and 3 are not represented. On this limited basis, the work opens with a foundational prologue that grounds theology in a first complex principle and a univocal concept of being valid for God and creatures. The prologue defends the Scotist formal distinction in God, classifies theology as a science in itself but revealed and believed for the wayfarer, and develops a detailed theory of abstractive and intuitive cognition. In Book 1, Distinction 37 treats God's ubiquity and presence in time as relations of presentiality grounded in creatures, which preserves divine immutability. In Book 3, Distinctions 23–32 offer a treatise on the theological virtues, framed by whether they were all in Christ's soul. A theological virtue is defined by God as primary object and by being a principle of merit. The order among the virtues is ascribed to divine ordination, and faith is held compatible with evident science and subjected in the intellect. Hope is made a species of faith, and merit is located in the interior elicited act. Across the covered parts, Meyronnes resolves theological questions by distinguishing formal notions, modes, relations, and primary versus secondary objects, and he is critical of inherited arguments and common opinions.
claims: Theological discourse rests on a first complex principle and a univocal concept of being common to God and creatures.
The formal distinction is required to preserve non-contradiction and simplicity in God.
Divine predicates involving creatures, such as ubiquity, are relations grounded in the creature.
The theological virtues are defined by God as primary object and by being principles of merit, and are ordered by divine ordination.
Faith is compatible with evident scientific knowledge.

FrMS88-d1e8112.summary: Meyronnes treats distinctions 23–32 of Book 3 in a single question: whether all the theological virtues were together in Christ's soul. The question is posed through the tension between Christ as comprehensor and Christ as one able to merit, but it is developed as a ten-article general treatise on the theological virtues rather than answered directly. A theological virtue is defined by having God as its primary object and by being a principle of merit, which excludes deductive theology, metaphysics, and the light of glory. There are exactly three, and obedience, heroic virtue, latria, and wisdom are excluded or reduced to them. They are infused, reside in the superior portion of the soul, admit no mean, and have God as both object and end. On connection, Meyronnes reports the common denial but, holding that the moral virtues are connected through legal justice rather than prudence, sees no reason to deny the connection of the theological virtues; charity is the 'form of the virtues' only as regards merit. Their order is not natural but comes from divine ordination: faith is lost only by heresy, hope only by despair, and charity through mortal sin only demeritoriously. In passing he states that Christ had charity but not faith or hope. Faith, as firm adherence on authority, is compatible with evident science and is subjected in the intellect, with the will causing belief only by command. Hope is a species of faith. One habit of charity loves God primarily and neighbor secondarily. The commanded act of charity is distinct from its elicited act but adds nothing to merit.
claims: A theological virtue has God as primary object and is a principle of merit.
There are exactly three theological virtues.
The theological virtues are ordered among themselves only by divine ordination.
Christ had charity but not faith or hope.
Faith is compatible with evident scientific knowledge and is subjected in the intellect.
Hope is a species of faith.
One habit of charity loves God and neighbor.
Exterior commanded acts add nothing to the merit of the interior elicited act.

FrMS88-d1x707.summary: PARTIAL: this summary of Book 3 rests on only 1 of its 9 direct divisions, Distinctions 23–32. Distinctions 1–22 and 33–40 are not yet interpreted and are not represented here; on the EDF they include the Incarnation and Christology as well as the moral virtues and gifts. The covered division is a single question on whether all the theological virtues were in Christ's soul, which Meyronnes turns into a general treatise on faith, hope, and charity. He defines a theological virtue by God as primary object and by its being a principle of merit. He fixes their number at three and their distinguishing properties (infused, in the superior portion of the soul, without a mean, with God as object and end). He makes their mutual order a matter of divine ordination rather than nature, and holds that Christ had charity without faith or hope. He reconciles faith with evident science and places faith in the intellect, with the will acting only by command. He makes hope a species of faith, assigns one habit of charity to love of God and neighbor, and denies that exterior commanded acts add merit to the interior elicited act. Here, as elsewhere, Meyronnes works by distinguishing formal notions, primary and secondary objects, and elicited and commanded acts, and he reports common opinions without simply deferring to them.
claims: A theological virtue has God as primary object and is a principle of merit.
The order among the theological virtues comes from divine ordination, not their nature.
Christ had charity but not faith or hope.
Faith is compatible with science and subjected in the intellect.
Merit lies in the interior elicited act, not in exterior commanded acts.
